name: Rotterdam
tagline: The city that rebuilt itself as the future
intro: On 14 May 1940 bombs flattened Rotterdam's old heart. Instead of copying the past, the city invented a new skyline — and kept a few survivors that tell the whole story, from Erasmus to the emigrant ships.

lessons.title: A city without a heart
lessons.hook: Near the Maritime Museum on Plein 1940, a tall bronze figure throws its arms up at the sky.
lessons.challenge: Look closely at the figure's body. What is missing?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the heart is missing (a hole in the chest).
hints: Walk around the statue and look at its chest.
The city's nickname for it is 'city without a heart'.
lessons.story: On 14 May 1940 German bombers destroyed Rotterdam's medieval centre. About 900 people died and tens of thousands lost their homes; the Netherlands surrendered the next day. The sculptor Ossip Zadkine saw the ruins in 1947 and made this figure, unveiled in 1953: a person with a hole where the heart should be, just as the city had lost its centre.

sources.label: Unveiling of The Destroyed City — Anne Frank House

lessons.title: The skyscraper that survived
lessons.hook: Find the white Art Nouveau tower by the Oude Haven, with little turrets on its roof.
lessons.challenge: When it was built, it was the first building of its kind in Europe. What kind?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says a skyscraper / high-rise.
hints: Count its floors and compare it with the buildings of 1898.
Today we'd call it a ten-storey tower.
lessons.story: The Witte Huis was finished in 1898. At about 43 metres and ten floors, it's often called Europe's first skyscraper — a 'hoogbouw' modelled on American office towers. In May 1940 it was one of the few buildings in central Rotterdam to survive the bombing, which is why it now looks so much older than its neighbours.

lessons.title: The scholar with a book
lessons.hook: Next to the big brick St Lawrence Church stands a bronze man in a long gown and a scholar's cap.
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says a book.
lessons.story: Desiderius Erasmus, born in Rotterdam around 1466, became the most famous scholar in Europe — witty, independent and a champion of learning. This statue by Hendrick de Keyser was unveiled in 1622 and is the oldest public bronze statue in the Netherlands. It survived the war. The church behind it, the Laurenskerk, is the last big medieval building in the centre: gutted in 1940, then rebuilt.

sources.label: Netherlands' oldest statue turns 400 — NL Times

lessons.title: Living in a tilted cube
lessons.hook: Look up at the yellow cubes balanced on their corners above the street.
lessons.challenge: Each cube is tipped onto one corner. By how many degrees is it tilted?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says 45 degrees.
hints: It's exactly half of a right angle.
lessons.story: Architect Piet Blom designed the Kubuswoningen as a village above the city: each house is a cube tilted 45 degrees on a six-sided pillar, and together they were meant to look like a forest. They were finished in 1984, though only 38 of the planned houses were built. People really live inside, with walls that slope in every direction.

sources.label: What are Rotterdam's Cube Houses? — Culture Trip

lessons.title: The Swan
lessons.hook: Walk onto the white bridge with the tall, bent pylon and its fan of cables.
lessons.challenge: Locals gave the bridge an animal nickname because of its shape. What animal?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says a swan.
hints: Look at the pylon from the side: long white neck, bent head.
lessons.story: Designed by Ben van Berkel and opened in 1996, the Erasmus Bridge links the old centre to the south bank. Its bent white pylon looks like the neck of a swan — hence 'De Zwaan'. The bridge helped turn Kop van Zuid, a run-down harbour district, into a new part of the city.

sources.label: The best of Rotterdam's architecture — Culture Trip

lessons.title: The building of goodbyes
lessons.hook: At the tip of the Wilhelminapier, find the building with two copper-green towers — once the head office of a famous shipping line.
lessons.challenge: Most ships that left from here sailed to one city — today it's the building's name. Which city?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says New York.
hints: Read the big letters on the roof.
lessons.story: From 1901 this was the head office of the Holland America Line. For decades, emigrants from all over Europe spent their last night nearby before boarding ships to New York; the line carried close to two million people to new lives across the Atlantic. The company moved its head office to Seattle in 1977, and in 1993 the building reopened as Hotel New York.

sources.label: Hotel New York fact sheet — Holland America Line

lessons.title: The Pilgrims' last harbour
lessons.hook: Take the metro or tram west to Delfshaven, the old harbour the 1940 bombs missed, and find the church on the quay.
lessons.challenge: In 1620 a famous group of English Protestants sailed from this quay on their way to America. What are they called?
lessons.rubric: Correct if the player says the Pilgrims / Pilgrim Fathers.
hints: The church is named after them.
They're remembered every Thanksgiving in the US.
lessons.story: The Pilgrims had lived in exile in Leiden. In the summer of 1620 they prayed on this quay, then sailed on the Speedwell to England, where they moved to the Mayflower and crossed to America. The church is now known as the Pilgrim Fathers Church, and Delfshaven is one of the few corners of old Rotterdam to survive the war.
